summary: This RFC specifies the Reliable Data Protocol, which gives packet-based applications a reliable data transport service. It was a proposal, and the authors asked for discussion and suggestions. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RDP carries separate messages between two processes and tries to deliver each one reliably. A connection can deliver messages in order or pass them to the application as they arrive.

reliable transport for packet based applications
how is rdp different from tcp

subtitle: A message-based transport that adds reliable delivery while allowing applications to choose ordering.

tldr.problem: Remote loading and debugging need messages delivered despite loss, while avoiding retransmitting every later message when only one segment is missing. Some applications also do not need ordered delivery.
tldr.mechanism: RDP numbers and checks each segment, acknowledges received data, retransmits unacknowledged segments after a timeout, and can acknowledge out-of-order segments separately.
tldr.outcome: RFC 908 describes a proposed Experimental protocol and asks for discussion. It was later updated by RFC 1151.

today: RFC 908 is an Experimental proposal that requested discussion and suggestions. It was updated by RFC 1151.

sections.title: Why RDP Uses Messages
sections.content:
The Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) was designed for packet-based applications such as remote loading and debugging. It aims to deliver every message efficiently across networks where segments may be lost, delayed or received out of order.

RDP sends messages rather than a continuous byte stream. Applications may request sequenced delivery when they need messages in sequence-number order; otherwise, the receiver can deliver them in arrival order. The RFC contrasts this design with TCP, whose byte-stream service always preserves order.
sections.plainLanguage: RDP sends one application message in each segment. The application chooses whether received messages must be delivered in sequence or may be delivered as they arrive.

sections.title: Connections, Ports and States
sections.content:
An RDP connection is a full-duplex channel between two processes. Each side uses an 8-bit port number, together with the network addresses, to identify the connection. A passive Open waits for a remote request; an active Open contacts a specified host and port.

The connection moves through CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RCVD, OPEN and CLOSE-WAIT states. The opening SYN exchange establishes initial sequence numbers and negotiates maximum segment sizes and outstanding-segment limits. A Close request sends an RST and enters a timed CLOSE-WAIT state, so the user must ensure data has been delivered before closing.
sections.plainLanguage: The two endpoints open a connection and exchange initial sequence numbers and limits. An application can listen for a connection or open one to a named remote host and port.

sections.title: Delivery, Acknowledgements and Flow Control
sections.content:
Each Send request becomes one segment with an RDP header and data. RDP does not split a large user message into smaller segments, so a message larger than the negotiated maximum segment size causes an error. Sequence numbers, a 32-bit checksum, acknowledgements and retransmission timers support reliable delivery.

A cumulative ACK identifies the last segment received in sequence. An EACK can list segments received out of sequence, allowing the sender to retransmit only missing segments. Each endpoint also sets a limit on the number of unacknowledged segments it can accept; the limit is agreed during connection setup and stays fixed for that connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver confirms data that arrived and can separately list correctly received segments that arrived out of order. If a segment is still unacknowledged when its timer expires, the sender sends that segment again.

sections.title: The RDP Header and Segment Types
sections.content:
Each segment begins with a variable-length RDP header. Its fixed fields include control flags, a version number, header length, source and destination ports, data length, a 32-bit sequence number, a 32-bit acknowledgement number and a 32-bit checksum. The checksum covers both header and data.

SYN carries connection setup information; ACK acknowledges in-sequence data; EACK adds sequence numbers for out-of-sequence segments; RST resets or closes a connection; and NUL checks whether the other endpoint is active. The RFC describes RDP over the IPv4 header but leaves the IP protocol number as “???”.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the connection and the segment's sequence and acknowledgement numbers. Flags show whether it opens, acknowledges, resets or checks a connection.
